A technical posture is a mechanical summary of indicator states — not a forecast, and not investment advice. Every row carries two independent reads: the six-family score (MACD, RSI, Bollinger, MA cross, SuperTrend, candlesticks) and the selected indicator set, split into a moving-average trend gauge and an oscillator gauge. Each band's measured historical edge is printed below so you can judge it on evidence. Vectora's separately-validated model probability lives on the daily brief.

Does the posture mean anything? — measured, not asserted

Every rating in this table was replayed across 13 years of DSE history and scored against what actually happened next: did the stock gain 5% within 10 trading days? “Edge” is the band’s hit rate minus the market’s own base rate over the same windows.
How much of that edge is real. This label rewards any stock that moves, so part of the edge is simply volatility rather than direction. Ranking stocks by trailing volatility alone — which knows nothing about direction — scores +10.8pp against the gauge’s +7.9pp: the dumb control wins. Comparing each stock only against others of similar volatility leaves a genuine +3 to +5pp, steady across all ten volatility bands. Treat that as the real number and the column below as its flattering upper bound.

Read with care: this measures whether price touched +5% at any point in the window, which is not the same as a profitable round trip — it ignores costs, slippage and exit timing. It also assumes every one of these instances was tradable at the shown liquidity.

Do the 21 indicators beat the six? — measured on 1,058,841 symbol-days

The same replay, applied to the 13-average and 8-oscillator set the client selected. The summary gauge’s Strong Buy carries a larger edge than the six-family Strong Buy (+8.4pp vs +5.9pp), so the second read earns its place. Two results deserve scepticism rather than excitement: the oscillator gauge beats the base rate at both extremes, and its Strong Sell (+8.8pp) reads better than its Buy (+1.3pp). That is not directional skill — a stock whose oscillators are screaming in either direction is simply a volatile stock, and this label only asks whether price touched +5%. Read the oscillator gauge as a volatility flag; read the moving-average gauge for direction.

Sector rotation — relative strength, not raw return

In a rising market almost every sector goes up, so raw return says little. Relative strength is the sector’s 21-day return minus the market’s over the same window, and momentum is whether that lead is still growing. A sector ahead but decelerating (Weakening) and one behind but accelerating (Improving) are usually the two that matter. Sectors are equal-weighted so a few giants cannot stand in for the whole group.
